title: Epistemic Laundering and the Persistence of Scientific Racism
abstract: Abstract Existing scholarship has documented the numerous methodological flaws as well as the social harms of hereditarianism. However, it has been less successful in explaining why such claims retain scientific credibility. I argue that this persistence is sustained by a structural process, which I call epistemic laundering: the acquisition and retention of scientific standing through circulation across settings governed by heterogeneous evaluative norms – including journals, conferences, and para-academic dissemination platforms – without a corresponding increase in the integrated warrant for treating the claims as reliable. I identify and analyse five laundering mechanisms: inferential-package fragmentation, category mobility, conceptual flipping, controversy laundering, and infrastructure bridging. I organise them into two conceptual clusters: evaluation-evasion mechanisms, which shape how assessment is distributed, deflected, or reallocated, and credibility-transfer mechanisms, which move and amplify credibility across institutional boundaries, converting fragmented local adequacy into the appearance of global scientific standing. I illustrate these mechanisms at two analytically connected scales drawn from intelligence research: the broader Human Diversity Foundation infrastructure, and the Pesta et al. (2020) meta-analysis in Intelligence. I conclude by examining editorial governance, the limits of refutation, and provenance disclosure as structural remedies.
